source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC)
finding: CompressARC solves ARC-AGI-1 puzzles by minimising the description length of the single target puzzle at inference time. No pretraining, no dataset, no search beyond gradient descent. The answer grid is left unconstrained and filled in by the compressed model.
numbers: 76K parameters. 2000 Adam steps per puzzle, about 20 min on one RTX 4070. 20% on the 400 public eval puzzles, 34.75% on the 400 training puzzles (2 guesses).
quote: lossless compression during inference time is sufficient to produce intelligent behavior
limits: Public ARC-AGI-1 only. Needs a hand-built equivariant network. Compute per puzzle is large for a 76K model.
agent_relevance: A compression-based solver is a different kind of solver from an LLM. It could serve as an independent second opinion on grid puzzles, not on text.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - formal framing
finding: Framed as code golf: the shortest self-contained program that prints the whole dataset, with unsolved grids filled arbitrarily. A one-size-fits-all compressor picks program f and input s to minimise len(f)+len(s). Algorithmic information theory says it is at most len(decoder code) bits worse than the best practical compressor.
numbers: Bound: at most len(f) bits worse. Program search is replaced by a VAE-style loss: KL of weights + KL of z + cross-entropy on known grids.
limits: The bound only means something if the decoder is short. The implementation does not count the length of the weights theta (regularisation off).
agent_relevance: Gives a clean statement of Occam's razor as a selection rule: prefer the answer that the shortest description of the whole puzzle implies.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - code length terms
finding: Three code parts: weights and inputs sent with relative entropy coding (cost = KL to a reference Gaussian), output corrections sent with arithmetic coding (cost = cross-entropy on the given grids). Reference for z is N(0,I). A weight reference N(0,I/2 lambda) turns the weight cost into L2 regularisation.
numbers: Loss = cross-entropy over the known grids (5 of 6 in the Color-the-Boxes example) + KL(z). The weight term is dropped.
limits: Authors say they do not use regularisation: 'Maybe it matters, but we don't know.' So the practical objective is not a full MDL.
agent_relevance: 'Minimise description length' in practice was a VAE loss. Our agent cannot do gradient descent, so only the selection idea transfers.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - results by compute
finding: Accuracy rises steadily with inference-time training steps and with the number of allowed guesses. Pass@n tables for 100 to 2000 steps.
numbers: Eval: step 100 pass@2 1.25%; step 500 pass@2 15%; step 1000 19.25%; step 2000 pass@1 18.5%, pass@2 20%, pass@10 26%, pass@100 31.25%, pass@1000 33.75%. Train pass@2 34.75%, pass@1000 52.75%. Time 6 to 138 h per 400-puzzle set.
limits: Pass@1000 is not the official metric.
agent_relevance: Test-time compute scaling exists for a compression solver too. The gap between pass@2 (20%) and pass@1000 (33.75%) means the right answer is often sampled but not selected.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - answer selection
finding: The answer grid depends on random z, so samples vary. The final answer is the most frequently sampled grid over training, with exponential-moving-average denoising as an aid. Single samples often have wrong colours on random pixels.
numbers: Eval pass@2 20% vs pass@1000 33.75%.
limits: Frequency voting inherits the usual weakness: a confident wrong mode wins. There is no independent verifier.
agent_relevance: Matches our guardrail that code, not the model, selects by frequency; but agreement is a hint, not proof (G4).

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - case study Color the Boxes
finding: On puzzle 272f95fa the KL falls to zero in almost all tensors of z except four that carry the rule: row positions, column positions, a direction-to-colour table and a colour tensor. PCA shows the code is human readable.
numbers: Top principal component is 1485x (rows), 1253x (columns), 829x (direction-colour) stronger than the next. Correct colours appear around step 350; model is final by step 1500.
limits: One hand-picked puzzle. In some replications a needed tensor fell to zero KL and the answer was then not recovered.
agent_relevance: The learned code is a short, inspectable rule. Suggests asking our agent to state a rule in few countable parts and to check that all parts are used.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - failure: posterior collapse
finding: Run-to-run variance: the same puzzle sometimes fails because a necessary tensor loses its information (posterior collapse). A KL floor was tried but did not help in practice.
numbers: Authors report they never saw a tensor recover after reaching zero KL. No numeric seed variance is given.
limits: Seed variance of overall accuracy is not reported.
agent_relevance: Compression solvers are high-variance per puzzle. Any use in our scaffold needs repeated runs and a count, not a single run.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - abilities and limits
finding: Can: colour assignment, infilling, cropping, connecting dots by lines (also diagonal), same-colour detection, adjacency, short translation. Cannot: two-colour mapping, repeated serial operations, counting, rotation, reflection, rescaling, duplication, connectivity, planning, long-range pattern extension.
numbers: Appendix H gives puzzle IDs, for example failures on 0d3d703e, 0a938d79, ce9e57f2, 7b6016b9, 2dd70a9a, 28e73c20.
limits: Limits come from the hand-built architecture, not only from MDL.
agent_relevance: Shows which task classes a compression view helps: local, perceptual, low-count regularities. Not counting, search or simulation.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - U-Net baseline
finding: A plain U-Net trained at inference time only on the target puzzle's demonstration pairs reaches 0.75% on the public eval set. Random augmentation made it worse on the training set (2.5% without, 1% with).
numbers: U-Net 0.75% vs CompressARC 20% (eval). 10000 steps; puzzles with a shape change were scored zero.
limits: Weak baseline, not tuned.
agent_relevance: Shows the compression objective plus symmetric architecture, not just 'train on the one puzzle', carries the result.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - comparison table
finding: Table 1 orders methods by training data used: brute-force rule search 40% (private eval); U-Net 0.75%; CompressARC 20%; HRM trained on test puzzles only 31% (ARC Prize ablation); HRM full 40.3%; OpenAI o3 high 87.5% (semi-private).
numbers: Same 2-guess scoring. Splits differ (private, public, semi-private), so numbers are not strictly comparable. Row alignment of the extracted table is my reading.
limits: Different splits and compute.
agent_relevance: Places the compression solver on the cost vs data frontier: low data, mid accuracy, high time.

source: Liao & Gu (2025) ARC-AGI Without Pretraining (CompressARC) - symmetry-breaking costs
finding: The architecture starts fully symmetric (example order, colours, rotations, flips). Using z to break a symmetry costs bits, and bigger symmetry groups cost more. So the cheapest explanation breaks the fewest symmetries.
numbers: 8 directions; multitensor reduced to 18 legal tensor shapes; one decoding layer only (a hierarchical VAE gave all the KL to the first layer).
limits: Design choice of the authors.
agent_relevance: 'Every distinction the answer needs must be paid for' can become a prompt rule: list the distinctions and prefer solutions that use fewer.

source: Akyurek et al. (2025) The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
finding: Temporarily updating an LLM on the demonstration pairs of each task (per-task LoRA, augmented, in-context formatted) lifts ARC accuracy several times. TTT is the main alternative to compression from scratch.
numbers: 80-task validation subset: fine-tuned 8B model 18.3% to 47.1% with TTT; 53.0% on full public validation with the BARC base; 61.9% ensembled with program synthesis. Semi-private eval 47.5%. BIG-Bench Hard 50.5% to 57.8% (10-shot).
limits: Relies on large pretraining on ARC-like synthetic data. Semi-private score is 14 points below validation.
agent_relevance: Inference-time learning helps when the base model has relevant priors. It needs weights that can be updated, so it does not apply to a prompt-only agent.

source: Akyurek et al. (2025) TTT ablations
finding: Each TTT design part matters. Removing geometric transformations loses 16 tasks (55%). Direct input-output formatting instead of in-context tasks loses 11 tasks (38%). A shared adapter instead of per-task loses 7 tasks (24%). Loss on demonstration outputs adds a little (26% to 29%).
numbers: Fine-tuned only 5% vs TTT 29% on the ablation subset (about 6x). 1B and 3B models reach the same accuracy after TTT; 8B fine-tuned alone 36%.
limits: Small 80-task subset: one task is 1.25 points.
agent_relevance: Augmentation matters as much as the gradient step, as in CompressARC (equivariance). For prompts: transform the problem and check agreement.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024 Technical Report
finding: Test-time training became the dominant approach to ARC-AGI-1 in 2024. All top LLM transduction solutions use it; no static transduction solution scored above 11%. TTT is described as shallow recombination of many building blocks by test-time gradient descent, the opposite end from program search.
numbers: Private eval: MindsAI 55.5% (not open), ARChitects 53.5% (1st place), Greenblatt 42%. Kaggle compute about $10 per entry. Estimated 85% for a Greenblatt-style method at about 100,000,000 programs per task.
limits: Report predates CompressARC and does not mention it.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold is closer to the program-search end; TTT is a second type; compression at inference is a third.

source: Chollet et al. (2025) ARC Prize 2024 - selection by stability
finding: The ARChitects chose among candidate outputs by their stability under augmentations (a selection criterion akin to a description-length proxy). Extra data: Re-ARC and ARC-Heavy/Potpourri (400,000 tasks).
numbers: NeMo-Minitron-8B base; 53.5% private eval.
limits: Details are in the team's own write-up, not opened here.
agent_relevance: Stability under transformation is a cheap, code-checkable selection rule that fits G3.

source: ARC Prize Team (2025) The Hidden Drivers of HRM's Performance on ARC-AGI
finding: Independent test of HRM. The hierarchy gives little; the outer refinement loop and training on the evaluation tasks' own demonstrations give most of the score. They say HRM is in effect zero-pretraining test-time training, like CompressARC.
numbers: Trained only on the 400 eval tasks: 31% pass@2 vs 41% original. Outer loops: 1 to 2 loops +13 points; 1 to 8 loops doubles the score. A plain transformer is within about 5 points. 300 augmentations suffice, not 1000.
limits: Blog analysis, not peer reviewed. Still shares weights across eval tasks; authors guess a strict per-task run would match CompressARC's 21%.
agent_relevance: Supports the claim that per-task learning, not architecture or cross-task transfer, carries performance. Iterated refinement from an own earlier output helps.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Hierarchical Reasoning Model
finding: HRM: 27M parameters, about 1000 training examples, reaches 40.3% on ARC-AGI-1 without pretraining or chain of thought.
numbers: ARC-AGI-1 40.3% vs o3-mini-high 34.5%; ARC-AGI-2 5.0%. 1000 augmentations per example.
limits: Later shown to owe little to the hierarchy (ARC Prize analysis).
agent_relevance: A small model trained on task demonstrations beats big CoT models on grids.

source: Jolicoeur-Martineau (2025) Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks
finding: TRM uses one 2-layer network that recurses on its own latent and answer. It beats HRM on ARC-AGI with 7M parameters.
numbers: ARC-AGI-1 44.6% and ARC-AGI-2 7.8% pass@2 (7M); HRM 40.3 / 5.0; direct prediction 21.0 / 0.0; Gemini 2.5 Pro 37.0 / 4.9; Grok-4-thinking 66.7 / 16.0. Sudoku-Extreme 87.4% vs HRM 55.0%.
limits: 1000 augmentations per task; ConceptARC added; not compression-based.
agent_relevance: The recursive self-refinement variant of inference-time work. Compare with CompressARC, which re-trains weights per puzzle.

source: Macfarlane & Bonnet (2024) Searching Latent Program Spaces (LPN)
finding: Latent Program Network: a 178M model learns a latent space of programs and does gradient search over the latent at test time. A middle route between test-time fine-tuning and program search.
numbers: ARC eval exact match: at 2e13 FLOPs LPN 15.25% vs TTT 13.50%; at 2e14 15.50 vs 16.00; at 2e15 15.50 vs 15.25. In-distribution LPN 80.0 vs TTT 58.5 at 2e13. Out of distribution LPN doubles from 7.75% (2e11) to 15.5% (2e15).
limits: 2 days on TPU v4-32 on re-ARC; the eval set is far out of distribution. Gains saturate near 2e13 FLOPs and TTT catches up at high compute.
agent_relevance: Latent search at test time is cheaper than fine-tuning at low compute. The compute-accuracy curve has a knee.

source: Macfarlane & Bonnet (2024) LPN - pattern task OOD
finding: On a synthetic pattern task out of distribution, in-context learning and TTT fail while latent search works, and accuracy grows with the number of inference gradient steps.
numbers: OOD exact match: in-context 0.0; TTT 0.0 / 1.8 / 0.3 at Grad 0 / 10 / 100; LPN Grad 1: 59.9% (10 steps) and 88.0% (std 5.3, 100 steps). Mean of 3 seeds.
limits: Toy 10x10 grid task, 3 seeds.
agent_relevance: A fixed-weight forward pass cannot scale its compute; test-time search needs a structure that makes search effective.

source: Li et al. (2025) Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
finding: Neural induction (write a program) and transduction (predict the output) solve different ARC problems, and which problems each solves is stable across seeds. Ensembling approaches human level. TTT on the transduction model is a large part of the gain.
numbers: Validation, 2 tries: transduction no TTT 39.25%, with reranking 43.0%, TTT without reranking 56.75%; induction (20k samples, majority vote) 35.25%. Average human 60.2%, best humans 98%. Later ensemble with Akyurek TTT: 61.9%.
limits: Trained on synthetic Python variants of ARC training tasks; ensemble choices tuned on validation.
agent_relevance: Induction and transduction are complementary; a compression solver is a third error profile that may add independent signal. Not tested.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) Language Modeling Is Compression
finding: Prediction and lossless compression are equivalent through arithmetic coding. Large LMs are strong general compressors, and in-context learning is a form of compression. When model parameters are counted, the adjusted rate is far worse.
numbers: Chinchilla 70B compresses ImageNet patches to 43.4% and LibriSpeech to 16.4% of raw size, better than PNG 58.5% and FLAC 30.3%. enwik9 raw: Chinchilla 70B 8.3%, Llama 2 7B 8.9%, gzip 32.3%.
limits: Raw rate ignores model size; Chinchilla may have seen Wikipedia, so enwik9 is not clean out-of-distribution.
agent_relevance: Any LLM's log-loss on a puzzle is a code length. An agent could score candidates by log-likelihood, but this is a proxy biased by training exposure.

source: Deletang et al. (2024) - model size vs dataset size
finding: The adjusted compression rate depends on dataset size. Larger models win only on larger data; on small data the model's own size outweighs the gain. There is a critical model size per dataset.
numbers: Model size in bytes is twice the float16 parameter count; the optimum shifts with enwik7, enwik8, enwik9.
limits: Small Transformers trained on one corpus; empirical.
agent_relevance: For one puzzle the data are tiny, so the model must be tiny (CompressARC 76K). A big LLM's fit to one puzzle says little by itself.

source: Havasi et al. (2019) Minimal Random Code Learning (MIRACLE), citing Hinton & van Camp (1993)
finding: Weights stored with noise cost KL(q||prior) bits (bits-back argument). The ELBO equals negative description length. MIRACLE encodes a weight sample with a random code. CompressARC builds on this line.
numbers: LeNet-5/MNIST and VGG-16/CIFAR-10: best test performance for a fixed memory budget (Pareto). 1 nat = 1.44 bits.
limits: The 1993 paper was not opened; its content is read through this paper. This is weight compression, not puzzle solving.
agent_relevance: Formal base of 'learning as compression' used by CompressARC.

source: Kingma & Welling (2014) Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes
finding: The VAE loss is reconstruction error plus KL to a prior, which can be read as a code length. CompressARC's decoder is a VAE decoder with a custom equivariant network.
numbers: Training objective: ELBO.
limits: Not about ARC.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Chollet (2019) On the Measure of Intelligence
finding: Defines intelligence as skill-acquisition efficiency using algorithmic information theory, and introduces ARC. This is why per-task learning from few examples is the test for compression solvers.
numbers: ARC: 400 training tasks, 400 evaluation tasks, plus hidden tasks.
limits: Position paper; no solver.
agent_relevance: Frames why a solver that learns from only the given examples is the right comparison.

source: Sun et al. (2024) Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States
finding: Makes the hidden state a small model updated by a self-supervised gradient step on each token. Inference-time learning inside the layer lowers perplexity as context grows.
numbers: 125M to 1.3B parameters; TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP keep reducing perplexity past 16k context where Mamba does not.
limits: TTT-MLP has memory I/O problems; language modelling, not reasoning.
agent_relevance: Inference-time learning in language models is a general mechanism, not specific to ARC.
